I was curious about this movie because of a ridiculously enticing trailer that had Leonard Cohen 's " You want it Darker " playing over it. The lyrics seemed perfect for the images I was seeing on screen : "There's a lover in the story, but the story's still the same - There's a lullaby for suffering and a paradox to blame - I didn't know I had permission to murder and to maim - You want it darker ? We kill the flame." Well, I wish I had never seen that trailer. Because, truly, nothing was remotely as good as what those 2 minutes teased and suggested. [Spoilers ahead] ( Before I start - I know that this is adapted from a book, and I've seen, as always, people say that the book was better, but know that I am not aware of the differences bewteen the original story and its adaptation.) THE PLOT : Against her father's rules, Maren, 18, sneaks out of the house to join a slumber party with 3 other girls. She must go back ' before 6AM ' she says, just in case. We barely have any time to get to know any character, our protagonist included, that she bites off her friend's finger. She comes back home, bloodied, banging on the front door. Her dad, instantly, gives her a " You didn't ", confirming this wasn't a first. " You have 3 minutes to pack before we leave and the police comes ". This clearly isn't a first. Maren and her father flee, and start a new life, all over again. But soon enough, her dad disappears. Maren is left all alone with her 'issue', with, as a goodbye, a message on a cassette to listen to, and a birth certificate with her estranged Mother's name. Here starts the girl's journey to find the latter, and herself alongside. THE CAST : Probably my very first problem with this movie - None of the characters I felt invested in, and the second roles shone way more than the 2 protagonists, Maren ( Taylor Russell ) and Lee ( Timothée Chalamet ). They are lifeless, boring, unconvincing. They have about as much chemistry as water and oil do. We're somehow supposed to believe those two love each other to death in such a short time, and while I know young love can be intense, this is not what's accurately represented here. Lee and Maren are together by default , because ' they're the same '. That's all. We don't see them having any real meaningful conversations, we just see them be . Which again, would be fine if they had that spark, but they just do not. THE SFX : The very few gory scenes are very well executed and I honestly wished there would have been more. For a movie which the literal main theme is cannibalism, there is almost none of it on screen (or off, for that matter). THE SOUND : Oh man, that fucking acoustic guitar. Those damn 4 accords we keep hearing all throughout the movie just about drove me crazy. Every time a conversation ended, or an important scene did, we had those zoom outs accompanied by that guitar trying to be melancholic. Of what , exactly ? I couldn't tell you. This movie desperately tries to be mellow, bittersweet and contemplative, but it fails in all regards. It's just slow and vapid. You should have seen the face I made when I recognized Trent Reznor 's voice at one point (in what I learned was the title song). I still cannot believe this literal genius of a composer did this score. If it wasn't for (obviously) hearing his voice; I would have never associated Reznor (nor Atticus Ross) to this movie. THE CINEMATOGRAPHY : This is the only good part of this movie, the way it looks. If you look at the trailers, it is absolutely beautiful, the dialogue sounds heartfelt, the feelings of the characters seem intense, it looks so good. Sadly, when spread accross two excruciating hours and eleven minutes, the cinematography isn't going to be enough. Despite it being gorgeous, I still have some gripes with it; to me, the filming lacked any kind of dynamism - it actually does feel like a 2h music video at times. And believe me, I love contemplative films. This one just wasn't it for me. IN THE END : Bones and All seems like a failed promise. From the moment Maren meets Lee, the movie ironically goes downhill. It wants to be controversial but just doesn't go far enough, then take that back and tries throwing us off with disgusting, shocking  characters, but they're never an actual threat. It all falls short. And every time the protagonists do something reprehensible, they are excused, justified by their ' nature ' and the very quick and basic remorse Maren sometimes shows. Their personal set of morals is discussable too; as the only person we see the couple feeding on together is a gay guy that Lee kills in a cornfield (only after sex, for some reason), but when Maren discovers he was married to a woman with a kid, suddenly, she freaks out. Ok girl. In the end, what bothers me most probably is the parallel this film obviously tries to make, using cannibalism as an analogy. The poster says " You can't run from who you are ", pretty much making them being cannibals their whole identity, making it unquestionnable, while the movie itself fights tooth and nails to make them appear desperately human. Final note : 2/10 . Bones and All had -everything-, and I truly mean everything , on paper, to appeal to me. But I found nothing enjoyable aside from the visuals, and then again, not for 2+ hours. As I often say to myself, " This would have been a great 40min short ".

Träumer Kino der schönsten und seltsamsten Sorte, das vielleicht gar nicht so das großartige Werk mit Metaphern aufgeladen ist, sondern eher eine kleine sympatische Kuriosität. Bones and All würde ist ein wenig bizarr und voller Gegensätze, aber im Kern würde ich sagen, es ist eine Außenseiter-Story, wie man ein Leben lebt mit einem let's call it "Lebensstil", der als problematisch angesehen wird. Dazu gehört sowas wie, dass sobald das Leben unerträglich wird, man Gleichgesinnte findet, die einem Halt geben, das Konzept fatalistischer Liebe und natürlich ganz viele Bilder, die ein Midwest-Roadtrip so gemütlich machen, wie man ihn sich nur vorstellt. Der krasse Gegensatz ist dann natürlich der Part, wo Maren und ihre vielen Bekanntschaften Menschen essen, aber auch das wird weirdly eklig faszinierend eingefangen und wirkt gegen Ende fast schon karthatisch. So ganz konnte ich mir keinen Reim auf diesen Aspekt der Geschichte machen, aber wie gesagt ist der Film sehr laid back und hat mir eher etwas Komfort mit dem Gefühl gegeben, wenn man im Leben einsam ist und sich anders und missverstanden fühlt. In gewisser Weise ist es auch ein Coming of Age Film. Aus Marens Perspektive beginnt ihr Leben erst so richtig, als ihr Vater sie zurücklässt und sie die Welt auf eigene Faust, ohne einen Vormund, entdeckt. Sie lernt noch viele andere Menschen wie sie kennen und irgendwann wird klar, dass im ganzen Land eine Art Community existiert, die ihre Dränge unterschiedlich ausleben, aber alle versteckt vor der allgemeinen Gesellschaft leben. An der Stelle geht der Lebensstil von Maren und Lee auch perfekt mit der im Midwest geprägten Armut einher. Man kann sich nirgends niederlassen, entwickeln, ist generell misstrauisch und kann morden und rauben wie es einem beliebt, weils eh kaum jemand nachverfolgt. Am Ende ist Bones and All für mich weniger Horror oder große Metapher als einfach ein stimmungsvoller Roadtrip über Einsamkeit, das Heranwachsen und das Bedürfnis, irgendwo dazuzugehören. Nicht jede Idee geht für mich komplett auf, aber Luca Guadagnino erschafft daraus so eine eigenartige Wohlfühlmelancholie, dass ich mich in der seltsamen Perspektive von Maren und Lee total verloren habe.

Beautiful film. Luca did such a good job at balancing romance and horror, which are two polar opposites. The feeding scenes of the eaters were disgusting and incredibly gruesome, but watching it still felt warm somehow. Maybe it’s the muted colors and the strings that recurred throughout the film. My God, it was beautiful. I can’t believe I didn’t appreciate it as much before as I do now. Whatever they’re doing, killing and eating people, is morally wrong and just blatantly evil, but I can’t help but root for Maren and Lee. Whatever they had felt so calm and true, and they were really only like that with each other. ‘Di ko magets mga nagsasabing wala silang chemistry, to be honest kasi … kita niyo ba mga halikan scenes nila hahaha? I wanted the film to end when they had normal lives. They looked so happy. But the ending just made everything so much more painful to watch, andddd I’d watch it over and over again. It was so beautiful. What they had was bound to end eventually. Sabi nga nila, “Let’s be them for a while .” It wasn’t meant to last because they were pretending all along. I do wonder if they really had a choice, though. Maren actively decides not to eat people, but she eventually succumbs to it. Maybe cannibalism is intrinsic to them. Maybe they can stop for a while, eat their hands or whatnot in hopes of saving the people they love, but it all surfaces eventually, which is heartbreaking because it gets in the way of so many beautiful things. Or maybe… maybe they had a way out; they just didn’t know how. Siguro dito hindi magiging applicable ‘yong “if he wanted to, he would” hahahah. Ano ‘yun, final act of love niya ay ipinakain sarili niya para maging part siya ni Maren forever? Alam ko namang madali lang para sa kanila, well, for most of them at least, na mag move on sa mga kinakain nila, pero kung ako si Maren, ‘di talaga ako makakausad after niyan. Hay buhay talaga. What a painfully beautiful ending.

“The world of love wants no monsters in it.” Até os Ossos é um filme que eu gostei bastante, mas com um nó atravessado que demorei pra nomear. Ele é lindo de ver, tem duas atuações que me seguraram, tem uma metáfora potente, e ainda assim eu saí dele sentindo que faltou alguma coisa pra ele virar a obra que claramente queria ser. Eu gostei mas com ressalvas. A história acompanha a Maren e o Lee, dois jovens que compartilham a mesma condição, são canibais por natureza. Luca Guadagnino transforma isso em um road movie pelos Estados Unidos dos anos 80, os dois cruzando estradas vazias, cidades pequenas, motéis, tentando existir num mundo que jamais aceitaria o que eles são. É um romance sobre dois outsiders se encontrando, se reconhecendo, e descobrindo que talvez não estejam tão sozinhos quanto pensavam. E é aqui que mora o que eu mais gostei. O canibalismo, no filme, é metáfora de ser diferente, de carregar dentro de si uma coisa que a sociedade lê como monstruosa, de amar e desejar de um jeito que o mundo insiste em condenar. A fala de Janelle diz tudo, o mundo do amor não quer monstros dentro dele. É sobre não caber, sobre ser empurrado pra margem por uma natureza que você não escolheu, sobre procurar outra pessoa que carregue a mesma fome pra não ter que carregar sozinho. Essa leitura é o que sustenta o filme. Mas é também na metáfora que mora parte do meu incômodo, e é um incômodo dividido. Porque o filme nunca decide de tudo o que o canibalismo é. Ora é símbolo do outsider, ora é vício, ora é o amor absoluto de se entregar por inteiro a alguém, e ao mesmo tempo é uma coisa literal. Essa indefinição é meio faca de dois gumes pra mim, parte dela é exatamente o que me agrada, essa abertura pra ler o filme de vários ângulos, mas parte dela me deixa incomoda, com a sensação de que o filme não sabe direito o que quer dizer com a própria imagem central. Senti que Até os Ossos quer ser coisas demais ao mesmo tempo. Ele é road movie, é romance, é terror, é coming-of-age, e nem todas essas peças encaixam com folga. Tem horas em que ele parece uma sucessão de cenas belíssimas que não terminam de formar um quadro só. Cada pedaço isolado funciona, a fotografia é deslumbrante, os momentos de terror são bons, o romance convence, mas o conjunto fica disperso, sem a coesão que faria tudo isso virar uma coisa inteira. Até os Ossos é um filme que eu gostei de verdade, que me deu imagens interessantes, com atuações de Timothée Chalamet e Taylor Russell que merecem o crédito. Só não me pegou por completo, porque ele se espalha demais.

Break it down to its constituents and we’re left with a largely asinine riff on the drug film. Junkies on the road, relapsing, rationalizing, self-destructing (and then mutually destructing); lost innocents in revolt against the world. Guadagnino twists it by making the addiction hereditary – he leans very much on the image of sexuality, to such a degree that this film sometimes takes on the image of a crude queer metaphor; he twists it further by making his addicts sadistic flesh-eaters. Despite some early pains in establishing a ‘grounded’, even ‘ethical’ approach to an obviously impossible problem (how can one eat the flesh of others without causing inexcusable harm?), Guadagnino will revel in vulgar and indulgent images of suffering: he will have his young lovers eat the body of a man not yet dead, who did nothing to deserve a torture so completely depraved. The film will later situate the blue Chalamet on a picturesque hillside, wondering if maybe he’s a bad person. His teenage-bride is quick to sooth him: of course not. This is a film whose stylistic credentials are so far removed from any kind of ethical compass that is can – in full earnest character – pose such a scene in almost direct sequence with the aforementioned brutality: and it should be noted that the moral problem faced by Chalamet is not that he brutally feasted on a man still breathing, but that he picked a man who happened to have a wife and family. (Which again becomes a rueful connexion to the queer reading: as though this pseudo-sexual encounter has broken up the model family.) The situation of the film becomes vapid: if we are to reduce it entirely to metaphor, it deals almost exclusively in soft-focus banalities; if we are to take it for its substance, it becomes indefensibly repugnant and entirely self-satisfied. Chalamet and Russell acquit themselves reasonably well (as they sit watching the cows, noting that they all have mothers and fathers); Rylance, on the other hand, turns in another insipid performance as a muttering, stuttering (stop me if you’ve heard this before) oddball, who later shifts into an unedited template of the incel rager. Rylance remains a capable actor – his recent run of Jerusalem is proof enough – but his screenwork has been dogged by a series of performances that lurch and die in the field of ‘guess the accent’. The film generally may resemble, in vague structural arrangement, Badlands ; and it may follow the rhythm of Bonnie & Clyde ; and then the visceral sensuality of Trouble Every Day but it is – much alike Gaudagnino’s Suspiria – an object almost wholly devoted to a certain kind of aesthetic presence. These people become pretty icons to situate before beautiful American vistas; their violence is represented in a kind of vulgar delight. The irony such a story would require – even buttressed against a genuine emotional register – is absent; a prime Jarmusch would have made of this material something funny and something moving. Instead we are faced with a grotesque display of beautiful people doing terrible things, and finding the heart to forgive themselves.

The memes will lose the fact that this Taylor Russell's movie though. And while it doesn't all work. Every part that does belongs to her. Allow me to explain... Russell stars as Maren and Bones and All is her story. She is shy at school. Her father (André Holland) locks her up at night. We soon learn why. In the world of this film, based on a 2016 novel by Camille DeAngelis, being an “eater” of human flesh is a hereditary condition. It comes with a keen sense of smell which allows the eater to find others like them but for the most veteran eater, an eater can also use their sense of smell to locate homes where someone inside does not have much longer in this world. Because Maren knows nothing of her mother, she thinks maybe this necessary hunger afflicted her, too. And she traverses all over the Great Plains and Great Lakes to find her. First, she meets Sully (Mark Rylance) an older, polite eater whose sense of smell gives him the vibes of a stalker. Despite Sully’s kismet feeling, it’s those stalker vibes (he keeps his victim’s hair to braid into a rope) that puts her back on the road where she eventually meets and falls for Lee (Chalamet). The flesh of the story is the growing fondness and love between the two young eaters. Lee takes Maren on the road to find her mother and she learns more about his former life, too. Back in Kentucky, Lee has a younger sister (Francesca Scorsese) who begs for him to come home. The lovers’ road trip follows a world-building section that is full of tension and well-executed mood. The world-building is the bones of the story. The bones are eerie, and the flesh is twee. It’s a mix that doesn’t always work but the chemistry between Russell and Chalamet is so strong that each cameo (including Michael Stuhlbarg’s) feels extraneous and disruptive. (Of all the cameos in Bones & All, Suspiria’s Jessica Harper fares best as Maren’s grandmother who cannot bring herself to openly talk about her daughter.) Russell portrays Maren as guarded but warm, with a good read on others. And Chalamet has punk swagger that goes beyond his pink hair and torn jeans. Like many young punks, he’s lashing out at a self-centered world until he’s understood and forgiven. In the end, Bones and All starts to run out of gas because—while people are killed and eaten— the film never becomes a lovers-on-the-lam movie so the tension, which was so pronounced at the start, dissipates. The love story is pleasant and will surely be memed with care and admiration (so too will a cornfield rendezvous where Chalamet takes his fresh prey). But it weirdly removes a sense of urgency that they could get caught. The two sides of the story also carry different looks. The opening is full of shadows and darkness, punctuated gorgeously by streetlights and bedroom lights—the places where Maren is escaping and plunging into the unknown. Once it becomes a love story, the look of Bones and All becomes more hopeful with blue skies and open roads. There is a message about needing to accept yourself in order to love someone else, which is tried and true. But, even though there is bloodshed on the screen and gnashing teeth in the sound design, the light overtakes the darkness too much. Perhaps this is due to almost every character we meet being an eater and so the societal structure that they’ve all run away from doesn’t ever make a threatful appearance. Vampire movies, which often incorporate a love story, are usually driven by the threat of discovery. The absence of that in Bones and All, despite leaving evidence all over the Great Plains, makes it a beautiful-looking movie that becomes too devoted to repeating the same note. There is no “all,” just bones.

Es ist nicht recht erklärlich, wie, aber auf irgendeine Weise hat Luca Guadagnino es geschafft, einen ausreichend großen Teil der Welt davon zu überzeugen, dass er ein ernstzunehmender Filmemacher ist. Vielleicht, weil er selbst so verdammt überzeugt davon ist. Man lädt ihn nach Venedig ein und zeichnet ihn auch noch aus. Immerhin versucht der selbsternannte Auteur diesmal nicht Filmgeschichte neuzuschreiben, sondern begnügt sich damit, ein Buch zu bebildern. Bei "Call Me by Your Name" hat das ja immerhin ganz gut geklappt. Und Teenieschwarm Chalamet hat er auch wieder im Gepäck. Aber leider nicht James Ivory. Stattdessen diesmal wieder David Kajganech, dem wir "Suspiria" und "A Bigger Splash" zu verdanken haben. Gott, steh uns bei. "Bones and All" ist eine Verfilmung des gleichnamigen Jugendromans von Camille DeAngelis und erzählt Marens Weg ins Leben. Die junge Frau sieht sich alleine auf der Welt, nachdem nun auch ihr Vater plötzlich entschwunden ist, weshalb sie nun nach ihrer Mutter suchen will, die sie bereits nach der Geburt verließ. Das Ziel ist dabei nicht ganz klar, doch kauft sich Maren ein Busticket und beginnt die Spurensuche. Auf ihrem Trip durchs amerikanische Hinterland trifft sie allerlei Gestalten, darunter den etwa gleichaltrigen Lee, ebenfalls ein Außenseiter und Einzelgänger. Er begleitet sie auf ihrer Odyssee und die beiden einsamen Wölfe kommen sich näher. Außerdem sind beide übrigens auch noch Kannibalen, das nur für die Akten. Ja, die Geschichte braucht ein bisschen lustvolles Knabbern, um immerhin ein paar Nervenenden zucken zu lassen. Denn ansonsten ist die Coming-of-Age-Fabel hier so sehr nach der Lehrbuchschablone gestanzt, dass man vor Déjà-vus fast einen Anfall erleidet. Die beiden einsamen Seelen finden einander auf dem langen Roadtrip, kämpfen zusammen gegen ihre Traumata, doch zusammen können sie stark sein. Tolles Anderssein, Selbstakzeptanz, Emanzipation von den Eltern. Man kennt es. Auch Mark Rylance als schräger Antagonistenvogel wirkt so literarisch, dass seine Vorhersehbarkeit fast eine unglückliche Art Suspense erzeugt. Die einzige interessante Figur ist Michael Stuhlbargs Hillbilly, die große originelle Idee der Adaption, der mit seinem eigentlich Nicht-Kannibalen-Freund den Titel gibt: Sie essen ihre Opfer mit Knochen. Das ist zugegebenermaßen wirklich unheimlich, vor allem durch die aufgekratzte Ruhe des wie immer brillanten Stuhlbargs. Hillbillys sind und bleiben der größte Horror Amerikas. Wobei sie auch das Einzige sind, was einen hier überhaupt an den Handlungsort erinnert. Denn ansonsten ist Guadagninos Amerika so sonnendurchflutet, als wäre man im mediterranen Sommerurlaub. Selbst die abgewracktesten Staaten des Mittleren Westens und die düstersten Südstaaten flirren so grün wie die Toskana oder ergießen sich als malerisches Sizilien. Aber wie schon in "Call Me by Your Name" muss man es Guadagnino lassen: So deplatziert dieses Gefühl hier auch sein mag, er formt es großartig. "Bones and All" macht tatsächlich über weite Strecken Spaß, einfach weil alles so schön anzusehen ist und der Sommer einen bis ins schmackhafte Knochenmark dringt. Der Handwerker Guadagnino ist nun einmal begabt und hat zauberhafte Ideen, wie etwa ein Nachtbad im Fluss, dass nur von buntem Feuerwerk beleuchtet wird. Hätte er mit dem unerträglich prätentiös-ödem "The Staggering Girl" für Valentino Haute Couture nicht schon das Gegenteil bewiesen, könnte man in dem Mann einen der großen Mode- und Werbefilmemacher unserer Zeit vermuten. Dennoch steckt in "Bones and All" ein unleugbarer Charme der Lebendigkeit, sodass man sich durch die nicht zu peinlichen Standardsituation sorgenlos treiben lassen kann. Und dann ist da halt eben noch der Kannibalismus. Ja, was soll man mit dem machen? Natürlich kommen jetzt die großen Deutschleistungskürsler und erzählen einem was von Körperlichkeit, fleischlicher Leidenschaft und Gefahr eines verzehrenden Begehrens. Das mag ja alles auf dem Papier schön und gut sein und man spürt förmlich Guadagninos eifriges Nicken. Aber alles, was Gudadagnino fabriziert, sind Gore-Effekte. Viel Blut gibt es, natürlich, und gerade zum Finale werden die Bilder durchaus albtraumhaft. Aber das ist alles nur Geisterbahn. Guadagninos Coming-of-Age-Romanze passiert in einem völlig anderen Kosmos als die saftige Knabberarie. All der sogenannte Körperhorror ist ein weiter Sprung zurück hinter alles, was ein David Cronenberg und Clair Denis über Jahrzehnte im Kino kultiviert haben. Man denke "Trouble Everyday", an "Crash". Bei Guadagnino fühlt man nichts. Die sensuelle Vermählung von Fleischeslust und Lust nach Fleisch, von Küssen und Beißen bleibt eine bloße Behauptung. Ironischerweise wird der Film in seinen blutigsten Momenten am blutleersten. Der ganze Kannibalismus ist nicht mehr als ein Gimmick für einen sonst eher banalen Film. Dass ein solcher Budenzauber noch begeistert, verwundet wenig in einer Welt, die Ducournaus zahme Kinderei "Titane" als verstörendes Wagnis feiert. Am Ende will einem noch jemand erklären, wie wahnsinnig progressiv eine junge emanzipierte schwarze Frau als Protagonistin ist. Es ist ein Kino der Rückschritte, das Ideenlosigkeit mit angeblicher Extreme kaschieren will. "Bones and All" ist ein konventioneller Teeniefilm, den man sich mal antun kann, der aber in keiner Form das coole, anarchische Lebensgefühl vermitteln kann, das er vermitteln will. "Bones and All" ist der uncoole kleine Bruder von "Near Dark". Aber immerhin ist er noch in der besseren Hälfte von Guadagninos Filmografie. Herzlichen Glückwunsch.

It's not quite explainable how, but in some way Luca Guadagnino has managed to convince a large enough part of the world that he is a filmmaker to be taken seriously. Maybe because he himself is so damn convinced of it. He's invited to Venice and even given an award. After all, this time the self-proclaimed auteur is not trying to rewrite film history, but is content to illustrate a book. After all, it worked quite well with "Call Me by Your Name". And he's got teenycrush Chalamet in his luggage again. But unfortunately not James Ivory. Instead, this time it's David Kajganech, to whom we owe "Suspiria" and "A Bigger Splash". God help us. "Bones and All" is a film adaptation of the young adult novel of the same name by Camille DeAngelis and tells Maren's journey into life. The young woman finds herself alone in the world now that her father has also suddenly disappeared, which is why she now wants to search for her mother, who abandoned her at birth. The destination is not entirely clear, but Maren buys a bus ticket and begins her search for clues. On her trip through the American backcountry, she meets all kinds of characters, including Lee, who is about her age and also an outsider and loner. He accompanies her on her odyssey and the two lone wolves become closer. They are also both cannibals, by the way, just for the record. Yes, the story needs a bit of lusty nibbling to make a few nerve endings twitch, after all. Because otherwise, the coming-of-age fable here is punched so closely to the textbook template that one almost suffers a seizure from déjà-vu. The two lonely souls find each other on the long road trip, fight their traumas together, but together they can be strong. Great differentness, self-acceptance, emancipation from parents. You know that stuff. Even Mark Rylance as the quirky antagonist seems so literary that his predictability almost creates an unfortunate kind of suspense. The only interesting character is Michael Stuhlbarg's Hillbilly, the adaptation's big original idea, who gives the title with his actually non-cannibal friend: They eat their victims with bones and all. It's admittedly genuinely creepy, especially with the chirpy calm of the as always brilliant Stuhlbarg. Hillbillies are and remain America's greatest horror. And they are the only thing here that reminds you of the location at all. Otherwise, Guadagnino's America is as sun-drenched as if you were on a Mediterranean summer holiday. Even the most washed-up states of the Midwest and the gloomiest Southern states shimmer as green as Tuscany or paint themselves as picturesque Sicily. But as in "Call Me by Your Name", you have to hand it to Guadagnino: as out of place as this feeling may be here, he shapes it magnificently. "Bones and All" is actually fun for long stretches, simply because everything is so beautiful to look at and the summer penetrates you to the tasty marrow of your bones. The craftsman Guadagnino is talented and has magical ideas, such as a night bath in the river that is only illuminated by colourful fireworks. If he hadn't already proved the opposite with the unbearably pretentious and boring "The Staggering Girl" for Valentino Haute Couture, one might suspect the man to be one of the great fashion and advertising directors of our time. Nevertheless, there is an undeniable charm of liveliness in "Bones and All", so that one can drift carefree through the not too embarrassing standard situation. And then there is the cannibalism. Yes, what can you do with that? Of course, now the eager English students come and tell you something about physicality, carnal passion and the danger of a consuming desire. That may be all well and good on paper and you can literally feel Guadagnino's happy nod. But all Gudadagnino fabricates are gore effects. There is a lot of blood, of course, and especially towards the finale the images become quite nightmarish. But it's all just a ghost train. Guadagnino's coming-of-age romance happens in a completely different cosmos than the juicy munchies. All the so-called body horror is a far leap behind anything a David Cronenberg and Clair Denis have cultivated in cinema over decades. Think "Trouble Everyday", "Crash". With Guadagnino, you feel nothing. The sensual marriage of carnality and lust for flesh, of kissing and biting, remains a mere assertion. Ironically, the film becomes most bloodless in its bloodiest moments. All the cannibalism is no more than a gimmick for an otherwise banal film. The fact that such hype still inspires is hardly surprising in a world that celebrates Ducournau's tame kindergarten play "Titane" as a disturbing venture. For sure, someone still wants to explain to you how insanely progressive a young emancipated black woman is as a protagonist. It is a cinema of regressions that wants to conceal a lack of ideas with alleged extremes. "Bones and All" is a conventional teen film that one can enjoy, but which in no way can convey the cool, anarchic attitude to life that it wants to convey. "Bones and All" is the uncool little brother of "Near Dark". But at least it's still in the better half of Guadagnino's filmography. Congratulations.

Cannibalism is one of my absolute favorite subgenres of horror, but considering how much it has been tackled over the decades, it has never really been definitively defined. There's lots of different takes on the practice of consuming human flesh. There's the tribal approach like in "Cannibal Holocaust" and its use as a survival tactic, featured in films like " Ravenous ." There's the ghoulish variety, such as backwoods families often found in Texas and prone to murdering victims efficiently with motorized weaponry. Then you have the stealthy suburban cannibal, which is sometimes used in cheeky satyrical horror that is attempting to draw out some sort of metaphor about conformity, as in Bob Balaban's "Parents." All of these different types come with the same horrific fear that their victims are consumed and, with most of the remains housed in satisfied tummies, are never heard from again, which I always found rather chilling. But there's something else that all these types of cannibals have in common, and that is that their eating habits are always choice. They don't have to eat people, but they want to. What makes Luca Guadagnino's BONES AND ALL so unique is that it attempts to offer a purpose for these beings, giving them rules and a mythology much like vampires and other supernatural creatures that Hollywood loves to draw from. Although the characters in this film are driven by a genetic hunger that they can't ignore, there's otherwise not much supernatural about them, as Luca presents an ensemble that are a lot like us and people we may know. The film centers around Maren (Taylor Russell), an 18 year old girl who goes on the run after the latest in a string of compulsive incidents that make it difficult to make friends at school. She's searching for a family and it isn't long before others of her kind find her. There seem to be a lot of "eaters" out there in the world, and they sometimes are able to literally sniff each other out. After an introductory encounter with Mark Rylance (really making a meal out of his role), she continues on her road trip before coming across Lee, played by Timothée Chalamet. This actor who seems to be well on the path to superstardom had somewhat failed to impress me in the years following his astounding arrival in Luca's "Call Me By Your Name." It's not that he had been doing bad work since then, but perhaps I'm not as responsive to his "over it" style that so many find so compelling. But here he has something to be angsty about, and his performance works as both dangerous rebel and depressed soul searcher. He and Russell make a great pair, and the two go out into the world trying to find a home while occasionally satiating their hunger. Along the way they'll meet a bunch of colorful characters, including a memorable fireside chat with Michael Stuhlbarg and David Gordon Green. I was very happy to see a small role for Jessica Harper, who Luca coaxed out of semi-retirement for what I thought was an obligatory and respectful cameo in his "Suspiria" remake. Here she gets a quality scene which leads to an even better one with Chloë Sevigny, which is right around when the film peaked for me. This road trip movie, which frequently feels like a parody of Malik's "Badlands" but with more flesh-eating, does spin its wheels after a while and you get the sense that it's not really going anywhere. Perhaps I would have liked it more if it had leaned even more abstract and arty, rather than delivering violent thrills when we've all gotten more comfortable the love story elements. A little of Mark Rylance goes a long way here, and he can't decide if he'd rather chew Maren or the scenery. I appreciate that this film goes for some grisly gore, but it doesn't always feel like it has a purpose other than to shock us. I would have liked more discussion between characters about what they like about the taste of us. We must be pretty good if we are best consumed raw and unseasoned. (who has time to cook?) This definitely has some nasty images of body munching, which were a bit too graphic for some attendees at Alice Tully Hall to handle tonight, triggering some of the meaner audience members to giggle at the sight of the squeamish waddling down the rows towards the aisles. I feel like the film either needed more or less of its violence, because what's there feels a little matter of fact and sometimes a distraction once the film has decided the characters have been developed enough and now they need something to happen to them. For all the facts and history we get about characters early on, that goes away after a few weepy monologues but I longed for a bit more discussion that attempted to cope with how they might manage to function in society while giving into their urges. I had a lot of fun with this film up to a point, but I feel like it changes what it purports to be about and never fully recovers. Still, this is going to be a great way to avoid Thanksgiving leftovers come late November. Gobble gobble gobble.

Venezia 79 Coverage - DAY 3 Shy cannibals make for a strange and provocative piece from director Luca Guadagnino. Bones and All takes an unexpected moral step, with regret bleeding into torn flesh and skin. Taylor Russell’s understanding of the prose on hand is just as important as her portrayal of Maren Yearly, a begrudging cannibal attempting to understand her need to feed. A desire to figure it all out is at the heart of Maren’s journey, but it is up to Guadagnino to show restraint in his storytelling. An adaptation that comes through as far removed from the text it hopes to understand – Bones and All may as well be its own, unique piece that muses not on veganism but on the freaks at the feast, those looking for their individuality with the cards stacked against them. In doing that, Guadagnino prepares a littering of graphic horror elements. They are as bloody and real as the feelings Yearly has for her condition. Is it a condition? Bones and All never reveals the inner workings, just the outcome. An explanation would be futile for Maren, whose mannerisms are like a polite infected member of the 28 Days Later population. Instead, the campfire cannibal chats between Lee (Timothée Chalamet) and Yearly provide ample qualities that describe conditional impact and outcome, not cause or correlation. Their need to feed is opened well with a lingering, brief commentary from Mark Rylance, who sets out such few details that they too may as well be shrouded in mystery. But they are enough to cling to, Guadagnino has given enough detail to hold onto. To hope for more is understandable, but impossible. Rylance, with a button-clad lapel and a Foghorn Leghorn accent, provides a haunting rendition of what could happen to Chalamet and Russell. His whispered, whistling voice and provocations are lingering despite his few sightings throughout. Rylance finds a love for the role, a challenging performance that provides some clarity to the chilling moments Chalamet attempts to bring to the table. His performance is impossible to remove from this blur of Martin Sheen’s work on Badlands. A whiny and troubled character whose conditions and issues never transcend how entitled he appears. Chalamet’s work is fine enough, but it is Russell who steals the show and uses the ample work Chalamet provides as a base for her own soul-searching performance. Michael Stuhlbarg provides a brief and exceedingly creepy role too. Surplus to requirement? Maybe so. But that is Guadagnino in motion. It would not be enough to adapt, he must overcome. So much to change and so many variables to experiment with. Acoustic tracks lingering underneath horrific details. A cannibalistic cameo from Chloë Sevigny amps up the horror inevitably tied into Bones and All, which is both sparing and overwhelming with its relation to the horror atmosphere. Guadagnino attempts to rely on technical flashes and keen wordplay to build tension, but they feel bloated and move away from the thriller at the core of this. Is there a thrill in going bones and all? His adaptation and cast move toward the mental strain of coming to terms with beliefs and needs out of our control, why does his direction not follow suit? Bones and All is a functional piece that has infrequent, spotty moments to it. If you liked this review, you can read more of my work on my website, Cult Following . Can’t wait for the Timothèe Chalamet fans to eat this one up and miss the point entirely by romanticising it.

Arguably, the rawness and messy nature of the plot might have been the intention after all Video Review: www.youtube.com/watch?v=7YJZskUdxzY Bones and All comes from director Luca Guadagnino, known for Call Me By Your Name, and the 2016 Suspiria remake. It stars Taylor Russel of Waves and the Escape Room films as well as Timothy Chalamet, who I probably don't have to introduce any further. Bones and All is mainly a coming-of-age road trip story with the added spice of cannibalism mixed in with a romance story and the quest to find yourself. Not having read the base material of the novel… of the same name, I can't comment on how well Guadagninoadapted the story. But at times, the characters felt quite constrained with certain moments we have to build towards whilst at other times the CMBYN energy of just floating in the present came through too. But Guadagninois really great at capturing that lost teen type of story and whenever the more plot-based story elements come into play, the film loses a bit of its quality. A big part of the film is dedicated to the proportionally frequent run-ins with other cannibals, which sometimes felt a bit overbearing, but connected to the theme of finding your own way in and outside of a new community as you grow up. Maybe idk… they also ate a bunch of people. Bones and All is not for the faint of heart with lots of blood and gore. But is somehow innocent, kind, and gentle with its characters. Giving them room to be vulnerable - maybe not with each other on-screen - but with the audience as we get to see them go on a very unique journey. Now like I mentioned before, there are a couple of moments where the plot is given a higher priority than the characters, which happens to be especially noticeable towards the end of the film and made it a considerable amount less enjoyable to me and left a bit of a twisted, sour aftertaste of the film in my mouth. Certain parts of the film are also a bit rushed but might have been part of the novel so they had to fit in here. Again, haven’t read the novel so I can’t say for sure, but just the impression I got from the pacing. BONES AND ALL is a simmer pot of teenage angst with cannibalistic tendencies and is fine entertainment, but if you are looking for a more tame, romantic version of a boy falling in love with a cannibal, you’ll have to stick with Call me by your Name.

Abbandonata dal padre a causa della sua natura, Maren intraprende un viaggio per scoprire l’origine dei suoi istinti cannibali. Lungo la strada conosce e si innamora di Lee, un ragazzo solitario e sensibile che condivide i suoi stessi impulsi. I due attraverseranno insieme l’immensità delle badlands americane nel tentativo di costruirsi un’esistenza normale. Ma per quanto si sforzino, saranno condannati a lasciare dietro di loro una scia di sangue. Può un film sul cannibalismo risultare delicato o addirittura poetico? Sì, se pensiamo che l’atto di mangiare qualcuno altro non è che l’espressione più radicale del desiderio del corpo altrui. In Bones And All il consumo di altri esseri umani va oltre l’incontrollabile urgenza carnale, diventando un mezzo di emancipazione dalla solitudine e di accettazione della propria condizione. Luca Guadagnino dirige, con l’eleganza formale che ormai lo contraddistingue, un road movie esistenziale a tinte horror (alcune scene sono davvero disturbanti!) intriso di romanticismo che, insieme a Call me by your name e We are who we are, va a formare un meraviglioso trittico sull’adolescenza in cerca di sè stessa.

Beautifully grotesque. A canibalistic love story road movie about the pain and destruction we inflict on those around us and those we love. Like most films that wade into the horrific, it’s a metaphor for something. If you read it as a metaphor for addiction it feels almost heavy handed. Mainly from Chalamet’s character talking about the high and rush he gets after feeding. But as a story about violence — violence as something stemming from intergenerational conflicts and trauma — from abusive fathers and mothers; passed on and on to daughters and sons — then, as a film, it has a lot more weight. Telling this story is Guadagino’s style, with zooms, stillness and some great little moments of dream sequence editing. He also cuts away to objects and establishing shots mid action sequence, which give you time to breathe and let the last few seconds sit with you for a moment. A truly great film, that of course deserved its standing ovation. (Finally, it’s just funny to note that we judge whether a film has been well received based on how long a bunch of celebrities stand up and clap for it! 8 minutes is a hilariously long time to be stood on the spot clapping…)
